## Does Defensive Driving Remove Points in New Jersey?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/new-jersey/does-traffic-school-remove-points

- **Points removed:** 2 (not the 3 many course ads imply), once every 5 years
- **The catch:** You must already have at least 2 points on your record when you complete the course
- **Ticket dismissal:** Not available through an online defensive driving course in New Jersey
- **Insurance benefit:** State-mandated discount of at least 5% (up to 10%) for 3 years; available once every 3 years
- **How the credit posts:** Your provider reports completion to the MVC in 7 to 10 business days; the MVC does not accept certificates you submit yourself
- **Insurance discount claim:** You DO submit the certificate to your insurer for the discount
- **Not eligible:** Commercial and out-of-state licenses
- **Separate program:** The 3-point Driver Improvement Program is classroom-only and MVC-initiated for drivers at 12 to 14 points
- **Course:** 6 hours, MVC-approved; typical cost $29 to $50
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Yes, two points, with more fine print per point than any state in the country. Let's clear the three big misunderstandings in order.

First, it's 2 points, not 3. New Jersey's MVC-approved online defensive driving course earns a 2-point reduction, once every five years. The 3-point figure floating around belongs to a different program, the Driver Improvement Program, which is classroom-only and which you don't choose. The MVC initiates it for drivers sitting at 12 to 14 points, the edge of suspension. If a website is promising 3 points off from an online course in New Jersey, close the tab.

Second, you need points to remove points. The 2-point credit only applies if you have at least 2 points on your record when you complete the course. A clean-record driver who takes the course banking a credit against a future ticket gets nothing; the credit can't go negative and it can't be stored. Time the course after the points exist, not before.

Third, no, it won't dismiss your ticket. New Jersey has no online-course dismissal mechanism, full stop. The ticket, the fine, and the conviction all stand, and your insurer sees them. What the course touches is the aftermath: the point total the state uses, since MVC surcharges start at 6 points in three years, and your premium, which brings us to the actual quiet value here.

New Jersey law mandates an insurance discount for completing the course: at least 5%, up to 10% depending on carrier, for three years, claimable once every three years. On New Jersey premiums, among the highest in the country, that's real money. Our data puts a typical 10-over ticket at a $96 fine and roughly $4,869 in three-year insurance exposure as a ceiling estimate, the widest fine-to-insurance gap of any state we track. A $35 course won't erase that, but a mandated discount working against the country's most expensive premiums is the best partial hedge on offer, and plenty of clean-record New Jerseyans should take the course for the discount alone.

One piece of process that trips people constantly: the point credit and the discount travel by different roads. Your course provider reports your completion to the MVC within 7 to 10 business days, and the MVC will not accept a certificate you mail in yourself. The insurer is the opposite: you send your certificate to them to claim the discount. Provider handles the state, you handle the insurance company.

One thing the course can't fix: New Jersey adds a flat two points for a conviction from any other state, whatever the offense, so [a ticket you picked up out of state](https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/out-of-state-ticket) lands on your record here regardless of how minor it was.

Every MVC-approved online course we track is compared on the New Jersey page.

- **Last verified:** August 2026

Six hours, the MVC's number for every approved course, and New Jersey pairs it with sub-$30 pricing that makes this the cheapest instructional hour anywhere in our coverage, roughly $4 to $5 per hour at the $24.95 to $29 courses in our latest pull.

Nothing about the six hours is deadline-driven for the standard use. There's no ticket being dismissed, so no court clock; you're taking the course for the 2-point reduction, if you're carrying points, or for the mandated 5 to 10 percent insurance discount, and completion simply starts whichever clock applies. Online progress saves, and the course divides into a weekend's worth of sittings without consequence.

The one piece of timing that does matter sits at the finish line, not inside the hours: the point credit only fires if you have at least 2 points on your record when you complete, so a driver taking the course for points should finish it after the points exist. The discount has no such condition, which is why the clean-record version of this purchase, six cheap hours every three years for a standing discount on New Jersey premiums, is the quiet best use of the course.

## How Often Can You Take Defensive Driving in New Jersey?

- **For the 2-point reduction:** Once every 5 years, and only if you have 2+ points at completion

New Jersey runs the same two-clock design as New York, with stingier settings on the points side.

Clock one: the 2-point reduction is available once every five years, and it only fires if you're carrying at least 2 points when you complete the course. Five years is a long interval for a small credit, which makes timing everything. A driver who takes the course reflexively after a first minor ticket spends the five-year slot on points that would matter least; a driver climbing toward the 6-point threshold where New Jersey's MVC surcharges begin is spending it exactly where it pays. Check your point total before you enroll for this reason, and remember the credit can't be banked in advance: no points on the record at completion, no reduction, slot potentially wasted.

The clocks run independently. A course taken in 2026 for the discount doesn't block a points-motivated course later; each benefit checks only its own history. Just route the paperwork correctly each time, provider to MVC for points, you to your insurer for the discount.

Yes, with the clearest eyes in the series about what you're buying.

## Does Defensive Driving Remove Points in New York?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/new-york/does-traffic-school-remove-points

- **Points reduced:** Up to 4, from the total DMV uses for suspension calculations
- **What it does NOT do:** Does not dismiss the ticket, does not remove the conviction, insurers still see it
- **Lookback:** Applies only to points from violations in the 18 months before course completion
- **Limits:** Cannot reduce below zero; no credit against future tickets; does not lift an existing suspension or revocation
- **Insurance benefit:** Mandatory 10% reduction in the base rate of liability and collision premiums for 3 years (Insurance Law §2336)
- **Who gets the discount:** The principal operator; show your certificate to your insurer within 90 days
- **Frequency:** Point reduction once per 18 months; retake every 3 years to keep the discount
- **Course length:** 320 minutes, DMV-approved PIRP sponsor
- **DMV update:** Sponsor reports your completion to DMV within 10 weeks
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Yes, sort of, and New York is the only state on this site where that's the honest answer.

Everywhere else, "traffic school" is really about the ticket. California masks it, Texas and Florida dismiss it. New York's Point and Insurance Reduction Program does neither. Your ticket stands. The conviction goes on your record. Your insurer sees it. What PIRP does instead is subtract up to 4 points from the total the DMV uses when it decides whether to suspend your license.

Read that carefully, because it's narrower than the course ads suggest. The reduction only touches points from violations in the 18 months before you finish the course. It can't take your total below zero, it can't be banked against your next ticket, and if your license is already suspended or revoked, completing the course changes nothing about that. The DMV says all of this plainly on its own PIRP page, which is more than most of the sites selling the course do.

So why take it? Two reasons, and the second one is the quiet star.

One, the suspension math. If you're carrying points and one more ticket puts you in dangerous territory, a 4-point haircut is real breathing room, and it's available once every 18 months.

Two, the money. Finish a PIRP course and New York law, Insurance Law section 2336, forces your insurer to cut the base rate of your liability and collision coverage by 10% for three years. Not may. Must. It applies to the principal operator of the vehicle, you claim it by showing your certificate to your insurer within 90 days of finishing, and you can retake the course every three years to keep it running forever. On a typical New York premium that's roughly $214 a year in our data, call it $642 across the cycle, for a 320-minute course that costs $24 to $60. Plenty of New Yorkers with zero points on their record take PIRP purely as an insurance play, and they're right to.

The course itself is 320 minutes by regulation, online through any DMV-approved sponsor, and the sponsor reports your completion to the DMV within 10 weeks. No court involvement at any point. That's the other thing that makes New York different: PIRP is between you, the sponsor, the DMV and your insurer. The ticket process runs on its own track, and if you want to fight the ticket itself, that's a plea or a hearing, not a course.

And PIRP only ever touches New York points. If [the ticket came from another state](https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/out-of-state-ticket), New York generally won't add points for it anyway — Canada aside — so there may be nothing for the course to reduce.

Every DMV-approved online PIRP sponsor we track is compared on the New York page, with current pricing.

**Sources:** NY DMV PIRP: https://dmv.ny.gov/points-and-penalties/point-and-insurance-reduction-program | NY Insurance Law §2336 (10% mandate) | Ticket Cost Study: https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/blog/true-cost-of-a-traffic-ticket

## How Long Is a Defensive Driving Course in New York?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/new-york/how-long-does-traffic-school-take

- **Course length:** 6 hours, the DMV's requirement for every approved PIRP and IPIRP course
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Six hours, whether you take it in a classroom or online through IPIRP, because the number belongs to the DMV's program requirements, not to any sponsor. Every approved course in the state runs the same length, which turns "which course is shortest" into a question with no answer and "which course is cheapest and least painful for six hours" into the real one.

Online, the six hours behave like New York wrote them for commuters: progress saves, sittings are yours to schedule, and sponsors break the material into timed sections so the total instruction time meets the DMV's requirement however you slice it. There's no court deadline pressing on you for the standard voluntary use, since no ticket is being dismissed; you're taking it for the point reduction, the 10% insurance discount, or both benefit clocks, and completion simply starts them.

One timing note worth six hours of your attention: the point reduction applies to violations in the 18 months before completion. Finish the course, then let the benefit do its lookback; a course finished before the points exist reduced nothing.

Every DMV-approved online course we track is compared on the New York page, and the two benefit clocks are laid out on our frequency page.

**Sources:** dmv.ny.gov PIRP

## How Much Does Defensive Driving Cost in New York?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/new-york/how-much-does-traffic-school-cost

- **Course price:** $24 to $60 across DMV-approved PIRP sponsors; fees set by each provider
- **Court fees:** None. PIRP never touches a court
- **Hidden costs:** None required; the certificate is part of the course
- **The return:** Mandatory 10% cut to the base rate of liability and collision premiums for 3 years (Insurance Law §2336)
- **Typical value:** Roughly $214 per year on an average New York premium, about $642 over the cycle
- **Course length:** 320 minutes, online through any DMV-approved sponsor
- **Renewal:** Retake every 3 years to keep the discount running
- **Last verified:** August 2026

New York is the only state where this question has a negative answer. The course doesn't cost you money over its life. It pays you.

Start with the sticker. PIRP sponsors set their own fees, and the DMV-approved online courses run $24 to $60, with I Drive Safely currently at $24. There's nothing else on the bill. No court fee, because PIRP never involves a court. No filing fee, no state surcharge, no driving record requirement. You take the 320-minute course, the sponsor tells the DMV, you show the certificate to your insurer. Done.

Then the return. New York Insurance Law section 2336 requires your insurer to cut the base rate of your liability and collision coverage by 10% for three years when the principal operator completes an approved course. Required, not offered. On a typical New York premium that's about $214 a year in our data, roughly $642 across the three-year cycle, against a course that cost $24. And you can retake it every three years and keep the discount running indefinitely, which plenty of New Yorkers with spotless records quietly do. As recurring financial decisions go, a 25x return every three years for five and a half hours of your time is hard to beat anywhere, let alone at the DMV.

If you're here because of a ticket, one calibration. PIRP doesn't dismiss the ticket or hide it from your insurer, so the fine and any rate impact from the conviction still happen. What the course adds is the mandatory 10% working against that increase, plus up to 4 points off the DMV's suspension math. The full mechanics are on our points page.

The upsells to skip: expedited certificates and printed copies. Sponsors report your completion to the DMV themselves, and a downloaded certificate satisfies your insurer.

Every DMV-approved online sponsor we track is compared on the New York page.

**Sources:** NY DMV PIRP: https://dmv.ny.gov/points-and-penalties/point-and-insurance-reduction-program | NY Insurance Law §2336 | Ticket Cost Study: https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/blog/true-cost-of-a-traffic-ticket

## How Often Can You Take Defensive Driving in New York?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/new-york/how-often-can-you-take-traffic-school

- **For the point reduction (up to 4 points):** Benefit available once every 18 months
- **For the insurance discount (10% for 3 years):** Retake the course every 3 years to keep it running
- **The course itself:** You can take it any time; it's the benefits that are rationed
- **Last verified:** August 2026

New York runs its two benefits on two different clocks, and plenty of drivers take the course on the wrong one.

Clock one, points: completing a DMV-approved Point and Insurance Reduction Program course reduces up to 4 points on your record, and that benefit is available once every 18 months. The reduction applies to points from violations in the 18 months before completion, so timing matters: take the course after the points exist. Points from a ticket you get next month aren't touched by a course you finished last week.

Clock two, insurance: the same course completion earns a mandatory 10% reduction on your liability and collision premiums, and it runs for 3 years. When the 3 years end, the discount ends, and the renewal move is simply taking the course again. For a lot of New Yorkers with clean records, this is the whole reason PIRP exists: a course every third year as a standing 10% line item against New York premiums, no ticket required.

Notice what that means in combination. A driver using the course for points in year one can retake it in year four for a fresh discount cycle, and the two uses don't interfere; the 18-month point clock and the 3-year discount clock run independently. The state doesn't limit how often you sit the course itself, only how often each benefit pays out.

What no frequency unlocks: dismissal. A New York ticket is never dismissed by a course, at any interval; the fine and conviction stand and the course works on the aftermath.

The full math is on our cost page, and every approved online PIRP course we track is compared on the New York page.

**Sources:** dmv.ny.gov PIRP | Insurance Law §2336

## Is a Defensive Driving Course Worth It in New York?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/new-york/is-traffic-school-worth-it

- **Verdict:** Yes, and uniquely, yes even with no ticket
- **What you spend:** $24 to $60 and six hours, once every three years
- **What it returns:** A mandatory 10% insurance reduction for three years on liability and collision coverage, on premiums averaging over $4,000; plus up to 4 points reduced when you need it
- **What it never does:** Dismiss anything; the fine and conviction stand
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Yes, and New York is the one state in this series where the answer doesn't depend on having a ticket at all.

The reason is the mandatory discount. Complete a DMV-approved course and New York requires your insurer to cut 10% from your liability and collision premiums for three years. New York's average premium in our data runs over $4,000 a year, and while the discount applies to the liability and collision portion rather than the whole bill, 10% of most of a New York premium for three years comfortably runs to several hundred dollars, often approaching four figures, against a course costing $24 to $60. That's why the steady-state New York move is a course every third year as a standing line item, clean record or not. Few purchases anywhere reliably return ten times their price by state mandate.

The ticket-driven version stacks on top: up to 4 points reduced, once every 18 months, applied to violations in the prior 18 months. Worth it for a driver whose total is climbing; irrelevant to a clean record, which loses nothing, because the discount pays either way.

The honest limit: nothing here shields you from the ticket itself. The fine, roughly $183 on a typical ticket in our data, and the conviction stand, and your insurer sees them. New York's course softens the aftermath; it never prevents it.

Approved courses are compared on the New York page; both benefit clocks are on our frequency page.

## Can You Take Defensive Driving Online in North Carolina?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/north-carolina/can-you-take-traffic-school-online

- **Online accepted:** Often, but never assume. Acceptance depends on your county and your court
- **The format question comes bundled with the length question:** 4 hours in Wake and Guilford, 8 hours elsewhere
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Often yes, but North Carolina is the one state on this site where we won't give you a blanket answer, because North Carolina doesn't have one.

Online defensive driving courses for North Carolina are widely available and widely used, with providers holding approvals at the county level. But whether an online certificate satisfies your obligation depends on who's asking for it. A court that agreed to dismiss or reduce your ticket sets its own terms, including format. The DMV's point-reduction path and its clinic have their own requirements. There is no statewide statement that every online course counts everywhere, so the confirmation step isn't caution theater, it's the actual system.

The good news: it's one question, asked once. Whoever required the course, court clerk or DMV, tell them which course you intend to take and ask whether it qualifies, and get the course length requirement in the same breath: 4 hours if your case sits in Wake or Guilford county, 8 hours anywhere else. The wrong format or the wrong length is the same wasted receipt.

And before any of that, make sure a course is even your best move; for most first NC tickets the courtroom PJC does more than any course can, covered on our points page.

## Does Defensive Driving Remove Points in North Carolina?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/north-carolina/does-traffic-school-remove-points

- **Points removed by a defensive driving course:** Usually none. NC's course is not a standalone points tool
- **The mechanism that actually protects you:** Prayer for Judgment Continued (PJC), a judge-discretionary court disposition
- **DMV point reduction via course:** Only with 7+ points on your record, a $40 DMV eligibility hearing, once every 5 years
- **Court dismissal via course:** Only with prior court permission, case by case
- **Course length:** 4 hours in Wake and Guilford counties; 8 hours everywhere else
- **Insurance discount:** North Carolina mandates none
- **Typical course cost:** $45 to $95
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Mostly no, and North Carolina is the state where believing the course ads costs you the most.

In most states on this site, the course is the tool. In North Carolina, the court proceeding is the tool and the course is an accessory. Here's the honest map.

The thing you've probably actually heard about is the PJC, the Prayer for Judgment Continued. It's not a course and no school can sell it to you. It's a request you make to the judge at your court appearance: enter no judgment on this ticket. Granted, the ticket generates no conviction for insurance purposes, which is the outcome every other state's traffic school is imitating. It's discretionary, it's rationed, for insurance purposes one per household every three years, and it only exists if you ask for it in court instead of paying the ticket online. If you take one thing from this page: don't just pay a North Carolina ticket before you've understood what a PJC could do for you.

So where does defensive driving fit? Two narrow places. First, some courts and prosecutors will agree to dismiss or reduce a charge if you complete a course, but that requires prior permission from the court, case by case, and depends on the violation, your record and local policy. Get the agreement first, then enroll, never the reverse. Second, the DMV runs a genuine point-reduction path, but read the fine print: you need 7 or more points already on your record, you pay $40 for a DMV eligibility hearing, and you can use it once every five years. That's a tool for drivers in real trouble, not for a first speeding ticket.

One more North Carolina quirk: course length depends on where you are. Wake and Guilford counties mandate a 4-hour course; every other county requires 8 hours. Check which version your court or the DMV expects before you buy anything, because the wrong one is worthless.

The money context makes the strategy obvious. A typical 10-over ticket runs a $203 fine and roughly $3,735 in three-year insurance exposure in our data as a ceiling estimate, and North Carolina mandates no insurance discount for course completion. The course costs $45 to $95 and, on its own, prevents none of that. The PJC, granted, can prevent nearly all of it. Spend your effort on the courtroom.

All of this assumes a North Carolina license. If you were [ticketed here on an out-of-state license](https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/out-of-state-ticket), or picked one up in another state, the PJC question and what North Carolina reports across state lines work differently — and that's its own tangle.

If a court has told you to complete a course, or you've secured a dismissal agreement, the approved online options are compared on the North Carolina page.

**Sources:** last verified 2026-08-13 | NC DMV: https://www.ncdot.gov/dmv/ | Ticket Cost Study: https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/blog/true-cost-of-a-traffic-ticket

## How Long Is Defensive Driving in North Carolina?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/north-carolina/how-long-does-traffic-school-take

- **Course length:** Depends on your county. 4 hours in Wake and Guilford, 8 hours everywhere else
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Four hours or eight, and the deciding factor isn't the school or the course tier, it's the county your case sits in. Wake and Guilford counties mandate a 4-hour course; every other North Carolina county requires 8. No other state in our coverage splits course length by geography this way, and it's the single most common way North Carolina drivers waste money on this: a Raleigh driver buying the 8-hour course they didn't need, or a Charlotte driver buying the 4-hour course that doesn't count.

So the sequence is fixed: establish which version your situation requires, from the court that's handling your ticket or the DMV if you're on its point-reduction path, then buy exactly that version. Providers sell both, at different prices, $27.95 to $59 in our latest pull, and a checkout page won't stop you from choosing wrong.

The hours themselves behave like everywhere else online: progress saves, sittings are yours, and the deadline belongs to whoever required the course.

And standing behind the whole question, as always in North Carolina: for most first tickets the courtroom PJC outperforms any course of any length, covered on our points page. Courses we track are compared on the North Carolina page.

- **DMV point-reduction path:** Add a $40 eligibility hearing fee, and it requires 7+ points on your record
- **The ticket you're avoiding:** A typical 10-over ticket runs a $203 fine and roughly $3,735 in three-year insurance exposure (ceiling estimate)
- **Last verified:** August 2026

North Carolina's course pricing has a wrinkle no other state on this site has: the price depends on your county, because the required course does.

Wake and Guilford counties mandate a 4-hour course. Every other North Carolina county requires 8 hours. Providers price the two formats differently, so the first question isn't which school, it's which county your case sits in. As of August 2026, iDriveSafely's 8-hour course, the version most counties need, runs $59, and Improv lists at $27.95. Prices move; treat these as a snapshot, and confirm the course length your court or the DMV expects before paying for either, because the wrong format is $30 to $60 spent on nothing.

Stack the rest of the costs by path. If a court has agreed to dismiss or reduce your ticket for a course, your cost is the tuition plus whatever the court's own process charges, which varies. If you're using the DMV's point-reduction route, add a $40 eligibility hearing fee to the tuition, and remember that path only exists for drivers with 7 or more points, once every five years. And if you're pursuing the mechanism that actually protects most first-time NC drivers, the Prayer for Judgment Continued, the course costs you nothing because it isn't a course; it's a request to the judge, and its price is showing up to court instead of paying online.

That last option frames the money properly. A typical 10-over North Carolina ticket runs a $203 fine and roughly $3,735 in three-year insurance exposure in our data as a ceiling estimate, and North Carolina mandates no insurance discount for course completion. A $59 course, on its own, prevents none of that. Spend on the course when a court or the DMV has told you it buys something specific. Spend your effort on the courtroom either way.

## How Often Can You Take Defensive Driving in North Carolina?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/north-carolina/how-often-can-you-take-traffic-school

- **DMV point-reduction course:** Once every 5 years, and only with 7+ points on your record plus a $40 eligibility hearing
- **PJC, the mechanism most drivers actually use:** For insurance purposes, once per household every 3 years
- **Court-permitted dismissals:** Per case, with prior court permission
- **Last verified:** August 2026

North Carolina rations three different things on three different clocks, and knowing which clock governs you is most of the strategy.

The course clock is the strictest: the DMV's point-reduction path is available once every five years, and it isn't for everyday tickets anyway, requiring 7 or more points already on your record and a $40 eligibility hearing before the course counts for anything. Five years is a long dormancy for a tool of last resort, which is exactly what it is: drivers who qualify are drivers whose next points carry real suspension risk, and the once-a-half-decade reduction should be spent accordingly.

The clock most North Carolina drivers should actually be watching belongs to the PJC, the Prayer for Judgment Continued, and it's not a course at all. For insurance purposes, a household gets one PJC every three years; use a second inside the window and the insurance protection evaporates for both. Household is the operative word: your spouse's PJC last year spends yours. Before requesting one in court, know your household's history, because a wasted PJC is the most expensive free thing in North Carolina traffic law.

Court-permitted course dismissals run per case with prior permission, and a court agreeing once implies nothing about next time.

Whichever clock applies, course pricing and the county-based 4-hour versus 8-hour split are on our cost page, and the full strategy picture is on our points page. Approved online courses are compared on the North Carolina page.

**Sources:** last verified 2026-08-13 | NC DMV: https://www.ncdot.gov/dmv/

## Is Defensive Driving Worth It in North Carolina?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/north-carolina/is-traffic-school-worth-it

- **Verdict:** For the course alone, mostly no. For the court strategy it supports, emphatically yes
- **What's at stake:** Roughly $3,735 in three-year insurance exposure (ceiling estimate) on a typical ticket, with no state-mandated discount to offset it
- **What prevents that exposure:** A granted PJC, which costs nothing but a court appearance
- **Where the $27.95 to $59 course earns its keep:** When a court trades something specific for it, or on the DMV's 7-point path
- **Last verified:** August 2026

This is the one state in the series where our answer about the course is mostly no, and it's the most useful answer on this page of the site.

Run the numbers the way the course ads won't. A typical North Carolina ticket carries roughly $3,735 of three-year insurance exposure as a ceiling estimate, one of the steeper bills in the country, and North Carolina mandates no insurance discount for completing any course. A $27.95 to $59 course, taken on its own initiative, prevents none of that exposure and removes nothing from an ordinary record. As a standalone purchase it returns approximately zero.

What's emphatically worth it is the thing the course sometimes rides along with: the court proceeding. A granted PJC can prevent the entire insurance consequence, a return that's effectively infinite against its price of showing up and asking, rationed at one per household every three years for insurance purposes. And where a prosecutor or judge trades a dismissal or reduction for a course, the course inherits the value of that deal, suddenly worth many multiples of its price because the court made it so. The DMV's point-reduction path, 7-plus points, $40 hearing, once every five years, is similarly worth it for exactly the drivers it's built for.

So the North Carolina rule: never buy the course first. Understand your courtroom options, then buy the course if and when it's the ticket to something.

The full strategy is on our points page; courses, when you need one, are compared on the North Carolina page.

## Can You Take Defensive Driving Online in Ohio?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/ohio/can-you-take-traffic-school-online

- **Online accepted:** Yes, for BMV-approved courses earning the 2-point credit
- **For court dismissals:** Format acceptance is each court's call; confirm with the clerk first
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Yes for the state benefit, and ask first for the court one.

Ohio's 2-point credit runs on BMV-approved courses, and approved online delivery qualifies; complete one and the credit applies the same as a classroom seat, once every three years. For that purpose the format question is settled and online is the practical default.

Where Ohio stays local is dismissal. Whether a court will trade a course for dismissing or reducing your specific ticket is that court's discretion, and so is which courses and formats it accepts for the deal. Before enrolling for a court purpose, one call to the clerk answers both questions at once: do you offer a course option, and does the online course I'm looking at qualify. Enrolling first and asking second is how Ohio drivers end up with a certificate their court won't take.

## Does a Defensive Driving Course Remove Points in Ohio?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/ohio/does-traffic-school-remove-points

- **Points removed by a defensive driving course:** 2-point credit toward your total, once every 3 years
- **What it doesn't do:** The conviction stays on your record; the credit doesn't erase the ticket or hide it from insurers
- **Ticket dismissal:** Sometimes, at the individual court's discretion; confirm with your court before enrolling
- **Course length:** 8 hours minimum, approved provider
- **Suspension context:** Ohio suspends at 12 points in 2 years
- **Typical course cost:** $25 to $50
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Ohio's answer is a modest yes, and modest is worth being honest about.

Complete an approved defensive driving course and Ohio grants a 2-point credit against your point total, available once every three years. That's the whole headline. The conviction stays on your record, your insurer still sees the ticket, and two points is two points, not a clean slate. Ohio built a small, sensible tool and the course ads selling it as a record-wipe are overselling.

What two points actually buys you is distance from 12. Ohio suspends a license at 12 points in two years, and if you're a repeat customer of the state's speed enforcement, a 2-point credit is the difference between a warning letter and a suspension hearing. Drivers sitting at 2 or 4 points get almost nothing from the credit today. Drivers at 8 or 10 should take the course this week.

There's a second, quieter use for the same course, and it's the one that can actually save you money on a fresh ticket: some Ohio courts will dismiss a citation or reduce the fine if you complete a defensive driving course, and some won't. It's genuinely court-by-court. Ohio has no statewide election right like Florida's or Texas's, so the move is to call the clerk on your citation before you pay, before you enroll, and ask whether the court offers a dismissal or diversion option involving a course. If yes, that's the valuable version and the course pays for itself several times over. If no, you're back to the 2-point credit and the math above.

Cost-wise this is one of the cheaper states, $25 to $50 for the 8-hour course, against roughly $1,563 in three-year insurance exposure on a typical 10-over ticket in our data as a ceiling estimate. The course won't make that exposure disappear the way an Arizona or Florida dismissal does. Think of it as cheap insurance against the next ticket rather than a cure for this one.

One caveat this page assumes away: it's written for Ohio licensees. If you were ticketed in Ohio but licensed somewhere else, the 2-point credit does nothing for you — there's no Ohio record for it to touch — and [what actually happens to an out-of-state driver](https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/out-of-state-ticket) is a different question entirely.

Every approved online course we track is compared on the Ohio page.

**Sources:** last verified 2026-08-13 | BMV: https://www.bmv.ohio.gov/ | Ticket Cost Study: https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/blog/true-cost-of-a-traffic-ticket

## How Long Is Defensive Driving in Ohio?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/ohio/how-long-does-traffic-school-take

- **Course length:** 8 hours for an approved course
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Eight hours, one of the longer courses in our coverage, attached to one of the smaller prizes, which is worth knowing before you start rather than at hour five.

Every approved Ohio course runs the same 8 hours, so schools compete on price, $27.95 to $39 in our latest pull, and on how bearable they make the sit, not on length. Online courses save progress, and eight hours divides naturally into three or four evenings.

Whether the hours are worth it depends on which door you're at. For the BMV's 2-point credit, eight hours for two points once every three years is a fair trade for a driver whose total is climbing toward Ohio's 12-point suspension line, and a shrug for a clean record. For a court that's offered to dismiss or reduce your ticket in exchange for the course, the same eight hours is the best deal in the state, and the court's completion deadline, not any state clock, is the one to write down.

## How Much Does a Defensive Driving Course Cost in Ohio?

- **The ticket you're avoiding:** A typical 10-over ticket runs a $121 fine and roughly $1,563 in three-year insurance exposure (ceiling estimate)

Ohio is one of the cheapest states in the country to take a defensive driving course, which is fitting, because it's also a state where the course buys you something modest.

The course itself runs $27.95 to $39 online for the approved 8-hour format, based on prices we pulled in August 2026, with Improv at $27.95 and iDriveSafely at $39. Prices move, so treat those as a snapshot rather than a promise, but the range has been stable and there's no reason to pay more than about $40 in Ohio.

Take it because a court has offered to dismiss or reduce your ticket, and the court may add its own program fee on top; that varies court by court, so ask the clerk for the full number when you confirm they'll accept the course at all.

The comparison that matters isn't Improv versus iDriveSafely, it's the course versus the ticket. Our Ohio data puts a typical 10-over citation at a $121 fine and roughly $1,563 in three-year insurance exposure as a ceiling estimate. Where a court will trade a dismissal for a $30 course, that's the best deal in the state. Where it won't, you're spending $30 on a 2-point credit, still worthwhile if your point total is creeping toward Ohio's 12-point suspension, close to pointless on a clean record.

## How Often Can You Take Defensive Driving in Ohio?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/ohio/how-often-can-you-take-traffic-school

- **For the 2-point credit:** Once every 3 years
- **Court-offered dismissals:** Per case, at each court's discretion, separate from the 3-year clock
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Once every three years for the thing Ohio actually promises, the 2-point credit against your total.

The three-year interval is the whole rhythm of Ohio's program. Complete an approved course, the BMV applies a 2-point credit, and the option goes dormant until three years pass. Since the credit is modest, the timing question matters more here than in bigger-credit states: a credit taken when you're sitting at 2 points is a credit you can't take eighteen months later when you're sitting at 10 and staring at Ohio's 12-point suspension line. If your record has a habit of collecting points, the credit is worth more later than sooner. If a one-off ticket is genuinely out of character, taking it now is fine; you'll likely never need it again.

Running outside that clock entirely: court arrangements. Where an Ohio court offers to dismiss or reduce a specific ticket in exchange for a course, that's a per-case deal between you and that court, and doing one doesn't consume your 3-year BMV credit. It's also not something you can schedule; it exists where a given court offers it, which is why the first call on any fresh Ohio ticket is to the clerk, not to a course checkout page.

Nothing about frequency changes what the course can't do: the conviction from a paid ticket stays on your record and visible to insurers however often you study.

Pricing is on our cost page, $27.95 to $39 as of August 2026, and every approved online course we track is compared on the Ohio page.

**Sources:** last verified 2026-08-13 | BMV: https://www.bmv.ohio.gov/

## Is Defensive Driving Worth It in Ohio?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/ohio/is-traffic-school-worth-it

- **Verdict:** Yes where a court offers a dismissal deal; otherwise a cheap maybe
- **What you spend:** $27.95 to $39 and eight hours
- **Court-deal version:** Can prevent roughly $1,563 in three-year insurance exposure (ceiling estimate), up to roughly 40x on the course price
- **Credit-only version:** 2 points off your total once every 3 years, the conviction and exposure untouched
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Depends which Ohio you're in, so here are both answers.

If a court has offered to dismiss or reduce your ticket for completing a course, yes, unambiguously. A $30-something course against roughly $1,563 of three-year insurance exposure at ceiling is up to roughly 40x on the money, and even a heavily tapered real-world surcharge leaves the trade lopsided in your favor. This version exists court by court, which is why the first move on any Ohio ticket is a call to the clerk asking whether it's on the table.

If no court deal exists and you're weighing the standalone 2-point BMV credit, the honest answer is: cheap, low-stakes, and worth it only when your point total says so. The credit doesn't touch the conviction or the insurance exposure; it manages license risk. At 8 or 10 points with Ohio's 12-point suspension looming, $30 and eight hours is obviously worth it. At 2 points on an otherwise clean record, you're buying a tool you probably won't need before it recharges in three years, and skipping it costs you nothing.

Eight hours is the real price for many people, one of the longer sits in the country, so let the point math, not guilt, decide.

Courses are compared on the Ohio page; both versions' mechanics are on our points page.

**Sources:** Ticket Cost Study: https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/blog/true-cost-of-a-traffic-ticket | BMV

## Can You Take Defensive Driving Online in Texas?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/texas/can-you-take-traffic-school-online

- **Online accepted:** Yes, statewide, for TDLR-approved driving safety courses
- **The order matters:** Get the court's permission for dismissal first, then take the course
- **Course:** 6 hours, minimum $25 by law
- **Not eligible at any format:** CDL holders (for dismissal)
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Yes. Texas accepts TDLR-approved online driving safety courses statewide, for both ticket dismissal and insurance discounts, and online has been the default way Texans take defensive driving for years.

The thing to get right isn't the format, it's the sequence. For a dismissal, you request the court's permission first, pay the court fee, capped at $10, and only then take the course by the court's deadline. Drivers who take the course before asking sometimes find the court won't apply it retroactively. Ask, then enroll.

Two Texas-specific rails: every provider must charge at least $25 by law, so a cheaper online course isn't a bargain, it's not a legal Texas course; and CDL holders can't use the dismissal at any format, online or classroom.

Every TDLR-approved online course we track is compared on the Texas page, with the full cost math on our cost page.

**Sources:** Art. 45A.352 | Educ. Code 1001.352

## Does Defensive Driving Remove Points in Texas?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/texas/does-traffic-school-remove-points

- **Points removed by defensive driving:** None. Texas has no license points system.
- **Points system status:** Repealed effective September 1, 2019 (HB 2048, 86th Legislature)
- **What the course does instead:** Full dismissal of an eligible ticket under Code of Criminal Procedure Art. 45A.352
- **Effect of dismissal:** Charge may not appear on your driving record or be used for any purpose (Art. 45A.357)
- **Frequency limit:** Once per 12 months, measured from the offense date
- **Not eligible:** Speeding 25+ mph over the limit, any speed 95+ mph, passing a stopped school bus, leaving the scene, work zone violations with workers present, CDL holders
- **Also required:** Proof of liability insurance
- **Request deadline:** On or before the answer date on your citation
- **Completion window:** 90 days from the court's order
- **Course length:** 6 hours, TDLR-approved
- **Minimum course price:** $25 by statute (Tex. Educ. Code 1001.352)
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Short answer: no, because there are no points to remove. Texas abolished its points system on September 1, 2019, when House Bill 2048 repealed the Driver Responsibility Program. DPS waived every outstanding surcharge on the same day. If a website is telling you how many points a Texas speeding ticket adds to your license, that page is at least seven years out of date, and there are several of them ranking on Google right now.

What you're actually worried about still exists though. A conviction goes on your driving record, your insurer sees it, and your rate goes up. The fix Texas gives you is better than point removal. It's dismissal.

Complete a TDLR-approved driving safety course with the court's permission and the charge is dismissed under Article 45A.352 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Not masked, not reduced. Dismissed. The statute says a dismissed charge may not be part of your driving record or used for any purpose. Your insurer never sees it because there is nothing to see.

The article number changed recently, by the way. Texas recodified the whole chapter effective January 1, 2025, and this dismissal is now Art. 45A.352 (courts cited the former article number for years). Same rules, new number. If your court paperwork shows the old citation, it is the same thing.

Here's how you qualify. You hold a Texas license or permit. You haven't used a driving safety course for dismissal in the 12 months before the offense date, and that clock runs from the ticket, not from when you finished the last course. You enter a plea of guilty or no contest and request the course in writing on or before the answer date printed on your citation. Miss that date and the judge can still say yes, but now it's discretion instead of a right. The court then gives you 90 days to finish the 6-hour course and get your certificate in.

One change from September 2025 that almost nobody has caught up with: if one stop produced more than one eligible ticket, Senate Bill 296 lets the court dismiss all of them off a single course completion. Before that it was one course, one ticket. If an officer wrote you up for two things at once, that amendment just cut your cost in half.

Not every ticket qualifies. Speeding 25 mph or more over the limit is out, and so is any speed of 95 mph or above regardless of the limit. Passing a stopped school bus, leaving the scene or failing to stop and give information after an accident, and violations in a construction zone with workers present are all excluded too. You also need to show the court proof of liability insurance to qualify, and the option isn't available to CDL holders at all. For the excluded stuff you're either paying, fighting it, or talking to the court about deferred disposition, which is a different mechanism with its own rules.

Cost-wise, the course itself runs $25 to $35. Texas law actually sets a $25 floor, so anyone advertising cheaper is making the difference up in fees. You'll also pay a court administrative fee, capped at $10, and you still pay court costs on the underlying ticket. All in you're usually out $60 to $90. Set that against what a conviction does to your insurance over three years and the math isn't close.

One more limit, and it's a hard one: the course requires a Texas license or permit, so if [you're licensed in another state](https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/out-of-state-ticket) you can't take it at all — no judge can waive that part, and active-duty military and their families are the only exception.

If you're ready to pick a course, we compare every TDLR-approved online provider on the Texas page, with current prices and what each one is actually like to sit through.

**Sources:** Art. 45A.351/45A.352/45A.354/45A.357 CCP: https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/CR/htm/CR.45A.htm | SB 296 (89th Leg.): https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00296F.htm | TDLR SB 296 notice: https://www.tdlr.texas.gov/news/2025/10/08/sb-296-relating-to-a-driving-safety-or-a-motorcycle-operator-training-course-dismissal/ | Exclusions per .gov courts: https://www.sugarlandtx.gov/177/Driving-Safety-Course , https://www.mctx.org/departments/departments_g_-_j/justice_of_the_peace_precinct_3/driving_safety_course.php , https://www.fortbendcountytx.gov/government/departments/justice-of-the-peace/precinct-1-place-2/driving-safety-courses , https://www.wilcotx.gov/627/Defensive-Driving | 90-day window (Art. 45A.354): https://www.victoriatx.gov/DocumentCenter/View/875/Drivers-Safety-Course-vs-Deferred-Disposition-PDF | $25 floor: https://www.tdlr.texas.gov/news/2025/08/27/driving-safety-providers-must-charge-students-a-fee-before-enrolling-them

## How Long Is Defensive Driving in Texas?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/texas/how-long-does-traffic-school-take

- **Course length:** 6 hours, set by Texas law, identical at every approved school
- **Not all of it can be video:** State rules cap audio/video content, so expect reading and interaction
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Six hours, and that's Texas law talking, not the school. Every TDLR-approved driving safety course in Texas teaches the same state-mandated 300 minutes of instruction, so a school advertising a faster course is advertising something that can't legally exist. Pick on price and experience; the clock is fixed.

What varies is how the six hours feel. Texas caps how much of the course can be audio and video, so even the slickest course mixes clips with reading, quizzes, and validation questions that confirm you're actually there. Online courses save progress, so the realistic pattern is two or three sittings across an evening or a weekend rather than one six-hour block.

The deadline wrapping the six hours belongs to your court: after granting permission to take the course, the court sets a completion date, typically 90 days. Six hours against 90 days is generous; the drivers who miss it are the ones who file the paperwork and forget.

Every approved online course we track is compared on the Texas page, and what the course actually buys is on our points page.

**Sources:** 16 TAC 84.505 | TDLR

## How Much Does Defensive Driving Cost in Texas?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/texas/how-much-does-traffic-school-cost

- **Course price:** $25 to $29 online across TDLR-approved providers we track
- **Statutory minimum:** $25 by law (Tex. Educ. Code 1001.352); anything cheaper isn't a TDLR course price
- **Court administrative fee:** Capped at $10 (Code of Criminal Procedure art. 45A)
- **Driving record:** Required for dismissal; the court can pull it for a fee, or you order it from DPS
- **Course length:** 6 hours, set by state rule
- **Typical all-in:** $60 to $90 including fees
- **What it prevents:** A conviction your insurer prices for 3 years
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Texas is the one state where the answer starts with a law instead of a sale banner. Providers must charge at least $25 for a defensive driving course. That's Education Code 1001.352, and TDLR reminded providers of it in writing last year. So every "cheapest course in Texas" claim collapses into the same $4 window: the courses we track run $25 at I Drive Safely and TicketSchool, $28.95 at Improv, $29 at Aceable. When the state sets the floor, price stops being the decision. Pick on format and hassle instead.

The course is only part of the bill though, and this is where most pages go quiet. When you request the course, the court can charge an administrative fee, capped at $10 by statute. You also have to produce your Texas driving record showing you haven't used this option in the past 12 months. Some courts pull it for you for a fee, otherwise you order it from DPS yourself. And some courts collect court costs at request time. Stack it up and a typical Texas dismissal runs $60 to $90 all-in.

Watch the add-ons at checkout. The statutory floor applies to the course, so the margin games move into extras: audio upgrades, same-day certificate delivery, bundled driving records at a markup. None of them are required. The 6-hour course and a certificate are the whole legal requirement.

Against that $60 to $90, the alternative is a conviction on your record that your insurer prices for three years. Our Texas data puts that exposure well into four figures as a ceiling estimate. This is one of the cheapest problems Texas will ever let you buy your way out of.

Every TDLR-approved online course we track is compared on the Texas page, current prices included.

**Sources:** $25 floor: https://www.tdlr.texas.gov/news/2025/08/27/driving-safety-providers-must-charge-students-a-fee-before-enrolling-them | $10 admin fee cap: https://www.txcourts.gov/media/1444617/j-ct-ct-cst-010118.pdf | Driving record mechanics: https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/79R/billtext/html/HB00703F.HTM | Art. 45A: https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/CR/htm/CR.45A.htm

## How Often Can You Take Defensive Driving in Texas?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/texas/how-often-can-you-take-traffic-school

- **For ticket dismissal:** Courts may grant a driving safety course dismissal once every 12 months
- **New since September 2025:** SB 296 allows one course to dismiss multiple eligible charges filed together
- **CDL holders:** Not eligible for dismissal regardless of timing
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Once every 12 months. That's the Texas clock on using a driving safety course to dismiss a ticket, and it runs from your last course-based dismissal, so the question a court asks isn't when you took the course, it's when a course last got a charge dismissed for you.

One genuinely new wrinkle makes the once-a-year math friendlier than it used to be. Under SB 296, effective September 1, 2025, a single course can now dismiss multiple eligible charges filed in the same case, where drivers used to have to pick one ticket and eat the rest. If you picked up two eligible violations in one stop, that's no longer a choice between them.

A few edges on the clock. The 12-month limit applies to the dismissal mechanism, so a court reviewing your request will check your record for a course dismissal in the preceding year. It's court-granted, not automatic: you request it, pay the court's fee, capped at $10 by state rule, and complete the approved 6-hour course by the court's deadline. And CDL holders are outside the program entirely, at any frequency, even for tickets in a personal vehicle.

If you're inside the 12-month window with a fresh ticket, the course route is closed but the ticket still has options, deferred disposition being the usual next conversation with the court. And if you're eligible, the math is on our cost page: about $25 to dismiss a ticket carrying real insurance exposure.

Approved online courses are compared on the Texas page.

**Sources:** Art. 45A.352 | SB 296 | txcourts.gov fee chart

## Is Defensive Driving Worth It in Texas?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/texas/is-traffic-school-worth-it

- **Verdict:** Yes, one of the clearest yeses in the country
- **What you spend:** Roughly $182 all-in, course, court fee and processing
- **What it can prevent:** Roughly $4,800 in three-year insurance exposure (ceiling estimate), about a 26x return
- **The conditions:** Court permission first, once every 12 months, no CDL
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Yes, and Texas is the state where the arithmetic barely needs an argument.

Run the whole trade honestly. Taking the defensive driving route costs roughly $182 all-in: the $25-and-up course, the court's fee capped at $10, and the associated processing. What it buys is dismissal, the charge resolved with no conviction for insurers to price. Our data puts the three-year insurance exposure on a typical Texas ticket at roughly $4,800 as a ceiling estimate, which makes the course route about a 26x return on the money spent. Insurance exposure is a ceiling, not a promise, since carriers vary and some taper surcharges, but even a driver whose real exposure lands at half the ceiling is looking at a 13x return on an afternoon.

The conditions are the usual Texas rails: the court grants the option, you ask before enrolling, it's available once every 12 months, and CDL holders are outside it entirely. Since September 2025, one course can even clear multiple eligible charges filed together, which only improves the math.

When is it not worth it? Almost never if you're eligible. The edge cases are drivers who'd contest the ticket outright and win, and drivers inside the 12-month window with no course option left.

## Can You Take a Driver Improvement Clinic Online in Virginia?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/virginia/can-you-take-traffic-school-online

- **Online accepted:** Yes, for most drivers, DMV-approved online clinics count for every clinic purpose
- **The two exceptions:** Drivers under 20 and CDL holders must attend in person
- **Same choose-one rule online:** Voluntary attendance buys safe driving points or an insurance discount, picked at enrollment
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Yes, with the cleanest carve-out in the country: everyone can take Virginia's driver improvement clinic online except two groups Virginia names outright, drivers under 20 and CDL holders, who are required to attend the classroom version, with commercial drivers taking the CMV-specific course.

For everyone else, a DMV-approved online clinic is a full equivalent. It satisfies court-ordered attendance where a court sent you, DMV-ordered attendance when point accumulation triggered it, and voluntary attendance for the safe driving points or the insurance discount, with the same rules riding along regardless of format: the fee can't exceed $100 by law, the voluntary benefit runs once every 24 months, and you still choose points or discount at enrollment, never both.

If you're in one of the two excluded groups, don't fight it with a workaround; the DMV tracks enrollment type, and an online certificate from an excluded driver doesn't satisfy the requirement. Classroom clinics are widespread and the obligation is the same 8 hours either way.

Every DMV-approved online clinic we track is compared on the Virginia page, the enrollment codes are decoded on our points page, and pricing is on our cost page.

## Does a Driver Improvement Clinic Remove Points in Virginia?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/virginia/does-traffic-school-remove-points

- **Points removed:** None erased. Virginia adds up to 5 safe driving points to your balance instead
- **How you enroll matters:** Four enrollment codes — court-ordered (COU), DMV-ordered (DMV), insurance (INS), voluntary (VOL) — with different benefits
- **The choose-one trap:** A voluntary clinic gives safe driving points OR an insurance discount, never both; you pick at enrollment
- **Frequency:** Voluntary safe-point credit once every 24 months; maximum safe-point balance is +5
- **Court-ordered attendance:** Court decides whether points are awarded; court-ordered drivers aren't eligible for the insurance discount
- **DMV-ordered attendance:** Triggered at 12 demerit points in 12 months or 18 in 24; 90 days to complete or suspension
- **Course:** 8 hours, DMV-approved; fee capped at $100 by law; online not allowed for drivers under 20 or CDL holders
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Virginia doesn't remove points. It runs a bank, and the answer depends entirely on which door you walk in through.

Start with the currency. Virginia assigns demerit points for violations, but it also maintains safe driving points, plus-one for each clean year, up to a balance of plus five. Complete a DMV-approved driver improvement clinic voluntarily and Virginia credits you up to 5 safe driving points, once every 24 months. Your demerits from the ticket don't vanish; your balance improves. A driver at minus 4 who takes the clinic can climb back toward zero. It's the most generous single credit in the country, Georgia's 7-point reduction aside, and most Virginians have no idea it exists.

Now the part that catches people. Virginia tracks why you enrolled, with four codes, and the code controls the benefit. Enroll voluntarily and you choose at enrollment: safe driving points or an insurance discount. One or the other, never both from the same attendance. Pick wrong and there's no switching after. If your record is carrying demerits, take the points. If your record is clean and you're purely rate-shopping, take the discount, and note the insurance track is for drivers 54 and under, with a separate mature driver course for 55 plus.

If a court sent you, different rules: the court decides whether you get safe driving points as part of your case, dismissal or fine reduction is at the court's discretion, and court-ordered drivers aren't eligible for the insurance discount at all. And if the DMV sent you, because you hit 12 demerit points in 12 months or 18 in 24, this isn't optional and there's no prize: you have 90 days to complete the clinic or your license is suspended.

The practical details. The clinic is 8 hours, Virginia caps the fee at $100 by law, and typical online tuition runs $45 to $75. Two groups can't take it online at all: drivers under 20 and CDL holders, who need the classroom version. Against a typical 10-over ticket, a $111 fine and roughly $1,707 in three-year insurance exposure in our data as a ceiling estimate, a $60 clinic that either restores your point balance or, where a court allows it, resolves the ticket itself is one of the easier calls in this catalog. Just decide which benefit you're there for before you type your card number, because Virginia will hold you to it.

And if the ticket itself came from outside Virginia, the clinic can't reach it: Virginia assigns demerits to [a conviction from another state](https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/out-of-state-ticket) just like an in-state one, but the credit only ever works on your Virginia balance.

Every DMV-approved online clinic we track is compared on the Virginia page.

**Sources:** last verified 2026-08-13 | VA DMV: https://www.dmv.virginia.gov/ | Ticket Cost Study: https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/blog/true-cost-of-a-traffic-ticket

## How Long Is a Driver Improvement Clinic in Virginia?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/virginia/how-long-does-traffic-school-take

- **Clinic length:** 8 hours, set by state requirement, at every DMV-approved clinic
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Eight hours, fixed by Virginia's clinic standard, whichever school delivers it and whichever of the four enrollment doors you came through. Court-ordered, DMV-ordered, insurance, voluntary: same clinic, same clock.

Virginia sweetens a long course two ways. The fee for the 8 hours is capped at $100 by law, with online clinics actually running $39 to $75, so the per-hour cost is among the lowest anywhere. And the prize scale matches the time: up to 5 safe driving points from a voluntary attendance is the most generous credit-per-course in the country, so Virginia is asking for a full workday and paying like it.

The hours come with one enrollment decision that outlasts them, choose safe driving points or the insurance discount before you start, and one hard deadline for the involuntary crowd: DMV-ordered attendees have 90 days from the order to finish their 8 hours or face suspension, which is ample and still routinely missed. Online progress saves for everyone eligible to be online, which excludes drivers under 20 and CDL holders, whose 8 hours happen in a classroom.

Every DMV-approved online clinic we track is compared on the Virginia page, and the four doors are decoded on our points page.

**Sources:** last verified 2026-08-13 | VA DMV

## How Much Does a Driver Improvement Clinic Cost in Virginia?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/virginia/how-much-does-traffic-school-cost

- **Typical course price:** $39 to $39.95 online for the 8-hour clinic
- **Examples as of August 2026:** iDriveSafely $39, Improv $39.95
- **The unusual part:** Virginia caps the clinic fee at $100 by law, the only price cap in our coverage besides Texas's floor
- **One attendance, one benefit:** Safe driving points or an insurance discount, chosen at enrollment, never both
- **The ticket you're avoiding:** A typical 10-over ticket runs a $111 fine and roughly $1,707 in three-year insurance exposure (ceiling estimate)
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Virginia is the rare state that regulates the price of the course itself: by law, a driver improvement clinic can't charge more than $100. In practice you'll pay well under half that. As of August 2026, iDriveSafely's approved 8-hour clinic runs $39 and Improv's runs $39.95, and the online market clusters in the $40 to $75 band. Prices move, so treat those as a snapshot, but anything approaching the $100 cap is buying you nothing extra; the clinic is standardized by the DMV and the certificate is the certificate.

What the money buys depends on the door you enter through, and Virginia makes you choose. Enroll voluntarily and your $40 buys either up to 5 safe driving points, once every 24 months, or an insurance discount, never both from one attendance, and you commit at enrollment. If a court sent you, the same tuition rides along with your case and the court decides what you get; court-ordered drivers don't qualify for the insurance discount at all. If the DMV ordered you in after too many demerits, the $40 isn't buying a benefit, it's keeping your license, and you have 90 days to spend it.

Two groups pay differently by necessity: drivers under 20 and CDL holders can't take the clinic online and need the classroom version, where pricing varies by location.

Against the ticket, the math is friendly. Our Virginia data puts a typical 10-over citation at a $111 fine and roughly $1,707 in three-year insurance exposure as a ceiling estimate. Where a court allows the clinic to resolve the ticket, $40 against $1,700 is a return few financial products offer. Even the consolation prize, 5 safe driving points restoring your balance, is the most generous voluntary credit in the country per dollar spent.

## How Often Can You Take a Driver Improvement Clinic in Virginia?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/virginia/how-often-can-you-take-traffic-school

- **Voluntary clinic for safe driving points:** Once every 24 months
- **Maximum safe-point balance:** +5, so back-to-back clinics can't stack beyond it
- **Court-ordered or DMV-ordered attendance:** As often as ordered; doesn't wait on the voluntary clock
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Once every 24 months for the version you choose; as often as ordered for the versions you don't.

Virginia's voluntary clinic, the one drivers take on their own initiative for safe driving points, runs on a two-year clock. Complete it, bank up to 5 safe driving points, and the voluntary option sleeps until 24 months pass. Two design features shape how to use it. First, Virginia caps your safe-point balance at +5, so a driver already at +5 gains nothing from a clinic; the two-year rhythm only pays if violations have eaten into your balance. Second, remember the choose-one rule from enrollment: each voluntary attendance buys safe driving points or an insurance discount, never both, so the 24-month interval is really rationing one benefit of your choosing at a time.

The involuntary lanes ignore that clock completely. If a court orders or accepts a clinic as part of resolving a ticket, that's per case, whenever cases arise. If the DMV orders you in after hitting 12 demerit points in 12 months or 18 in 24, the clinic isn't optional, isn't waiting on any interval, and comes with a 90-day deadline against suspension. Neither ordered attendance consumes your voluntary two-year slot, though the court decides what benefits, if any, attach to its version.

The steady-state pattern for a Virginia driver who collects the occasional ticket: let the clinic restore your balance every couple of years, and treat the $100 legal fee cap, detailed on our cost page, as the ceiling on what that maintenance ever costs.

Every DMV-approved online clinic we track is compared on the Virginia page, and the four enrollment doors are decoded on our points page.

**Sources:** last verified 2026-08-13 | VA DMV: https://www.dmv.virginia.gov/

## Is a Driver Improvement Clinic Worth It in Virginia?

**URL:** https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/virginia/is-traffic-school-worth-it

- **Verdict:** Yes, in every lane, with the court-permitted version among the country's best trades
- **What you spend:** $39 to $75, capped at $100 by law, and eight hours
- **Court-permitted version:** Up to roughly 24x against the avoided $1,707 three-year exposure (ceiling estimate)
- **Voluntary version:** Up to 5 safe driving points or an insurance discount, your pick, once every 24 months
- **Last verified:** August 2026

Yes, and Virginia is unusual in that the answer holds through every door you might enter.

The headline trade is the court-permitted one. Where a Virginia court allows the clinic to resolve a ticket, a course costing $39 to $75 stands against roughly $1,707 of three-year insurance exposure at ceiling, up to roughly a 24x return, plus whatever the court does with the fine. That version depends on the court's discretion, which makes the clerk conversation the first move, as everywhere.

But Virginia's distinctive value is that the fallback is genuinely good. Miss the court version entirely and the voluntary clinic still pays: up to 5 safe driving points, the most generous credit in the country, restoring a battered balance once every 24 months, or the insurance-discount track if your record is clean and you'd rather chip the premium. Eight hours and under $75 for either is solid value on its own terms, not a consolation prize. Even the involuntary version, when the DMV orders you in, is worth it in the bluntest sense: it's the price of keeping your license.

The only way to make Virginia's clinic not worth it is to fumble the enrollment choice, buying points you don't need or a discount you can't use. Decide which benefit you're there for before checkout, because that decision is final per attendance.

The four doors are decoded on our points page; approved clinics are compared on the Virginia page.

**Sources:** Ticket Cost Study: https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/blog/true-cost-of-a-traffic-ticket | VA DMV

---

## The True Cost of a Traffic Ticket (2026 study)

> TrafficSchoolPicker analysis of all 51 US jurisdictions. All-in cost of a first speeding ticket
> = fine + estimated 3-year insurance surcharge. Full write-up:
> https://www.trafficschoolpicker.com/blog/true-cost-of-a-traffic-ticket

- Nationally, one speeding ticket costs about $435 more per year in insurance (~$1,300 over 3 years). The average 24-25% rate increase dwarfs the ~$130 average 10-over fine.
- Most expensive states, all-in: Michigan $8,742, California $5,619, Hawaii $5,227, Texas $5,047, New Jersey $4,965, Delaware $4,582, Louisiana $4,512, Rhode Island $4,481, Nevada $4,228, Florida $4,170.
- Cheapest states, all-in: Vermont $1,305, Montana $1,486, Pennsylvania $1,494, Nebraska $1,528, Ohio $1,684, Utah $1,792, Virginia $1,818, Maryland $1,869, New Hampshire $2,024, Maine $2,100.
- Biggest traffic-school net savings: Michigan ~$8,600, California ~$5,300, Hawaii ~$5,050, Texas ~$4,650, Louisiana ~$4,300, Nevada ~$3,950, Florida ~$3,900, Tennessee ~$2,950, Arizona ~$2,950, Oklahoma ~$2,350.
- Texas example: a driving-safety-course dismissal (~$182 all-in incl. court fee + driving record) prevents ~$4,800 in 3-year surcharges, ~26x return. Mechanism is dismissal, not a discount.
- Course mechanisms differ by state: masking (CA, VC §1808.7), dismissal (TX, Art. 45A.352), adjudication withheld (FL, §318.14), base-rate discount (NY PIRP, insurers still see the ticket), one-time point masking (MI BDIC). PA/MA/NJ/KS offer little for a first ticket.
- Sources: FinanceBuzz (fines), CarInsurance.com/Quadrant (surcharges), U.S. News, NHTSA. Rankings are source-dependent (esp. Hawaii).
